content: If an expert is attempting to determine whether the combination of a patient’s race, age, and geographic region of residence is unique, they may utilize population statistics published by the U.S. Census Bureau to assist in this estimation. In cases where population statistics are unavailable or unknown, the expert may calculate and rely on statistics derived from the dataset itself. This is because a record can only be linked between the dataset and the population to which it is being compared if it is unique in both. By relying on the statistics derived from the dataset, the expert will make a conservative estimate regarding the uniqueness of records. For example, consider a dataset held by a covered entity that includes a record of a 25-year-old male from a specific geographic region in the United States. In reality, there are five 25-year-old males in that geographic region (i.e., the population). However, there is no readily available data source to inform the expert about the exact number of 25-year-old males in this region. By inspecting the dataset, the expert can confirm that there is at least one 25-year-old male in the population, but they cannot determine if there are more. Without additional knowledge, the expert assumes there are no more, treating the record in the dataset as unique. Based on this observation, the expert recommends removing this record from the dataset. In doing so, the expert has made a conservative decision regarding the uniqueness of the record. In the previous example, the expert provided a solution—removing a record from a dataset—to achieve de-identification. However, this is just one of many possible solutions that an expert could offer. In practice, an expert may provide the covered entity with multiple alternative strategies, based on scientific or statistical principles, to mitigate risk. They will attempt to identify which record in the dataset is most vulnerable to identification. However, in some cases, the expert may not know which specific record to be disclosed will be most vulnerable to identification. In such instances, the expert may compute risk from several different perspectives. The Privacy Rule does not mandate a specific approach to mitigate or reduce identification risk to a very small level. Instead, it allows for a variety of potential approaches. An expert may find all or only one method appropriate for a particular project or may use an entirely different method. If the expert determines that the risk of identification is greater than very small, they may modify the information to mitigate the identification risk to that level, as required by the de-identification standard. However, data utility does not determine when the de-identification standard of the Privacy Rule has been met. One class of identification risk mitigation methods corresponds to suppression techniques. These methods involve removing or eliminating certain features of the data prior to dissemination. For example, suppression of an entire feature may be performed if a substantial quantity of records is considered too risky, such as removing the ZIP Code feature. Suppression may also be applied to individual records, deleting records entirely if they are deemed too risky to share. This can occur when a record is clearly very distinguishing, such as the only individual within a county earning over $500,000 per year. Alternatively, suppression of specific values within a record may be performed, such as when a particular value is deemed too risky (e.g., “President of the local university” or unique ages or ZIP codes). Another class of methods involves generalization, which transforms data into more abstract representations. For instance, a five-digit ZIP Code may be generalized to a four-digit ZIP Code, which in turn may be generalized to a three-digit ZIP Code, and so on, to disclose data with lesser degrees of granularity. Similarly, a patient’s age may be generalized from single-year increments to five-year age groups. A third class of methods corresponds to perturbation, where specific values are replaced with equally specific but different values. For example, a patient’s age may be reported as a random value within a five-year window of the actual age. Similarly, the final digit in each ZIP Code may be randomized within a certain range. Perturbation is often performed to maintain statistical properties of the original data, such as mean or variance. The application of a method from one class does not necessarily preclude the application of a method from another class. For instance, it is common to apply both generalization and suppression to the same dataset.
